# BNGL language reference {#sec-bngl-reference}

```{python}
#| include: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "../scripts")
from bookutils import show_bngl, show_lines, model_path
from bngl_reference import native_model
import bngsim
import numpy as np

syntax = bngsim.Model.from_bngl(model_path("appendix_b", "syntax_demo"))
syntax.reset()
initial = bngsim.Simulator(syntax, "ode").run(t_span=(0, 0.01), n_points=2)
functional = native_model("functional_rates")
fd = functional["data"]["functional_rates.gdat"]
nf = functional["data"]["functional_rates_nf.gdat"]
```

BNGL describes molecular structures, patterns that select those structures,
and rules that change them. A file also contains actions that generate a
reaction network, run simulations, or export the model. The tables below
give the syntax used throughout this book; the accompanying files in
`models/appendix_b/` are executable examples.

The reference was checked against the
[BioNetGen source snapshot `9601746`](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/tree/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46)
and tested with BioNetGen `{python} functional['version']`. The parser
accepts some constructs that a particular simulator or exporter may handle
differently. Those distinctions are identified where they affect the
meaning of a model, especially in @sec-bngl-functional
and @sec-bngl-simulators.

## File structure and lexical conventions {#sec-bngl-file}

A model definition is enclosed by `begin model` and `end model`. Within it,
each block begins with `begin block-name` and ends with the corresponding
`end block-name`. Actions follow the model, either as individual commands
or inside `begin actions` and `end actions`. An explicit model wrapper is
recommended even though the parser also accepts older files without it.

| Block | Contents | Typical dependency |
|---|---|---|
| `parameters` | Numeric values and algebraic expressions | Define quantities before using them |
| `compartments` | Compartment names, dimensions, sizes, and containment | Declare enclosing compartments first |
| `molecule types` | Molecule names, component names, and allowed states | Define types before species and patterns |
| `seed species` | Fully specified initial molecular species and amounts | Requires parameters, types, and any compartments |
| `observables` | Patterns used to count molecules or complexes | Define observables before functions that use them |
| `functions` | Expressions that can depend on observables or time | Requires the referenced quantities |
| `energy patterns` | Structural patterns with free-energy contributions | Requires molecular types and energy parameters |
| `reaction rules` | Reactant patterns, product patterns, and rate laws | Requires the referenced definitions |

Some blocks are optional. For example, a model with mass-action rules
needs no `functions` block, and a spatially homogeneous model needs no
`compartments` block. Use the order above to make dependencies visible.
The `species`, `reactions`, and `groups` blocks also occur in generated
`.net` files; they describe an enumerated network rather than the compact
rule definition.

| Construct | Syntax and interpretation |
|---|---|
| Comment | `#` begins a comment extending to the end of the line |
| Continuation | A trailing backslash joins a logical statement to the next line |
| Identifier | Use a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits, or underscores; names are case-sensitive |
| Number | Integer, decimal, or scientific notation, such as `1`, `0.1`, or `1e-3` |
| Rule label | `Bind:` precedes a rule and names it in generated output |
| String | Quoted text in action arguments, such as `"ode"` or `"R(l)"` |
| Action options | `{name=>value,...}`; string values are quoted and arrays use square brackets |

Choose distinct names for parameters, observables, and functions since they
share the expression namespace. Parentheses enclose molecule components,
function arguments, and action arguments, with different meanings in each
context. Semicolons are unnecessary in the examples in this book.

The following file has the core blocks and an ODE action:

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "syntax_demo")
```

## Parameters, expressions, and units {#sec-bngl-expressions}

Each parameter line has the form `name expression`. The expression can
refer to previously defined parameters. A derived parameter such as
`KD koff/kon` records an algebraic dependence; observables that change during
a simulation belong in functions when they control a rate.

| Operation | BNGL syntax |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` |
| Grouping | `(expression)` |
| Comparison | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` |
| Logical combination | `&&`, `||` |
| Conditional | `if(condition,expression_if_true,expression_if_false)` |
| Exponential and logarithms | `exp(x)`, `ln(x)`, `log10(x)`, `log2(x)` |
| Magnitude and root | `abs(x)`, `sqrt(x)` |
| Trigonometric functions | `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan` |
| Hyperbolic functions | `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `asinh`, `acosh`, `atanh` |
| Aggregation | `min(...)`, `max(...)`, `sum(...)`, `avg(...)` |
| Nearest integer | `rint(x)`, implemented as $\lfloor x+1/2\rfloor$ |
| Mathematical constants | `_pi()`, `_e()` |
| Simulation time | `time()` in a dynamic expression |

Use `^` for exponentiation and explicit parentheses to clarify compound
conditions. Internal states such as `Y~p` are labels; they are distinct
from the numeric quantities used in expressions. Avoid undefined
operations, including division by zero and logarithms of nonpositive
values, in all reachable model states.

BNGL does not infer a unit system from parameter names. For an amount
variable $x$, a unimolecular rate coefficient has units of inverse time,
a bimolecular coefficient has units of inverse amount per time, and a
source rate has units of amount per time. Select concentration or molecule
count units and convert every parameter consistently.

`substanceUnits("Concentration")` and `substanceUnits("Number")` declare an
amount convention for processing and export. They do not perform an
automatic conversion of arbitrary seed amounts and kinetic parameters.
Stochastic simulation requires molecule counts and rates appropriate to
those counts. Compartment sizes and the amount convention together affect
compartmental scaling (@sec-bngl-compartments).

## Molecule types and molecular species {#sec-bngl-molecules}

A molecule type declares the components that can occur on a molecule and
the internal states allowed for each component:

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "syntax_demo", "begin molecule types", "end molecule types")
```

`R(l,d,Y~u~p)` declares a receptor with components `l`, `d`, and `Y`.
Component `Y` can have state `u` or `p`; a particular receptor has one of
those states. A component can carry both a state and a bond, as in
`R(Y~p!1).K(r!1)` if the declared molecule types allow that structure.

Repeated component names represent equivalent sites. For example,
`A(b,b,b)` declares interchangeable binding sites on `A`; the declaration
can compress symmetric interactions but also introduces matching
multiplicities. Distinct names such as `b1` and `b2` distinguish sites and
permit site-specific rates.

| Structure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `L(r)` | A ligand whose `r` component is unbound |
| `R(l,d,Y~u)` | A complete receptor with both binding components free |
| `R(l!1,d,Y~p).L(r!1)` | A receptor-ligand complex, with the bond endpoints sharing label `1` |
| `R(l,d!1,Y~p).R(l,d!1,Y~u)` | A dimer containing receptors in different internal states |
| `A(x!1,y!2).B(a!1).C(a!2)` | A connected complex with distinct labeled bonds |

A dot joins molecules within one species or pattern. Bond labels identify
the endpoints of an edge within that expression; reusing `!1` in another
expression does not connect the expressions. Each explicit bond has two
endpoints. Molecule order and bond numbering can change when BioNetGen
writes a canonical species string, while the molecular graph remains the
same.

A seed-species line has the form `complete_species amount`. Specify every
component and internal state needed to identify the species. A seed species
must be connected, so separate unbound molecules occupy separate seed
lines. A zero initial amount is useful when later actions must address
that species explicitly. Prefixing a seed species with `$`, as in
`$A() A0`, fixes the amount of that particular species. Complexes containing
the same molecule type are separate species and acquire their own amounts.

## Patterns and matching {#sec-bngl-patterns}

A **pattern** selects molecular structures by specifying some of their
properties. Components omitted from a pattern impose no condition on
their states or bonds. A component that appears without a bond annotation
is required to be unbound. These two forms therefore select different
sets of molecules:

| Pattern | Required properties |
|---|---|
| `R()` | A receptor in any internal state or binding context |
| `R(l)` | The `l` component is present and unbound |
| `R(l!+)` | The `l` component is bound, with the partner unspecified |
| `R(l!?)` | The `l` component may be bound or unbound |
| `R(Y~p)` | State `p` at `Y`, with `Y` unbound |
| `R(Y~p!?)` | State `p` at `Y`, with either bond status |
| `R(l,Y~p)` | Both named components are unbound and `Y` has state `p` |
| `R(l!1).L(r!1)` | A receptor bound to a ligand through the specified components |

If `Y` is purely an internal-state component in the model, its unbound
condition adds no restriction. When a component can also bind a partner,
include `!?` to select its state independently of binding. Omitting
`~state` leaves the internal state unspecified; `!?` refers to bonds.

Consider `R(Y~u) -> R(Y~p) kp`. The rule preserves omitted components and
their partners, so the phosphorylation event can occur in a ligand-bound
receptor or a dimer. Adding `l` to both sides restricts the rule to
receptors with a free ligand-binding component. Adding `l!+` restricts it
to bound receptors. Such unchanged requirements are the rule's context.

A pattern can have several embeddings in a species, for example when a
dimer contains several receptors in the required state. Those embeddings
can affect observable weights and reaction rates. The pattern attribute
`{MatchOnce}` restricts its matching to at most one embedding in a given
species. For example, `{MatchOnce}R()` requests one match per
receptor-containing complex. Apply it only when the intended event or
measurement is defined per complex; restricting a match that identifies
distinct reactive sites can remove physical events.

## Observables {#sec-bngl-observables}

An observable line has the form `type name pattern`, followed by any
additional patterns. Patterns may be separated by spaces or commas.

| Type or modifier | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `Molecules` | Sum the pattern embeddings, weighted by the amount of each species |
| `Species` | Count each matching species instance once per listed pattern, irrespective of that pattern's embedding multiplicity |
| `Species Pair R()==2` | Select species with exactly two embeddings of `R()` |
| `Species Cluster R()>2` | Select species with more than two embeddings of `R()` |

`Species` counts the amount of matching complexes. It does not report the
number of distinct species definitions in the generated network. For a
single-molecule pattern, `Molecules` counts molecules of that type. For a
multimolecule motif, it counts motif embeddings, which can include a
symmetry multiplicity. Quantifiers such as `==2` refer to the number of
embeddings of the preceding pattern; for `R()` this is the number of
receptors in a complex.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "syntax_demo", "begin observables", "end observables")
```

The seed mixture gives `Rtotal =`
`{python} f'{initial.observables["Rtotal"][0]:g}'` and `Rcomplexes =`
`{python} f'{initial.observables["Rcomplexes"][0]:g}'` in the chosen amount
units. Each dimer contributes its receptors to `Rtotal` and one complex
to `Rcomplexes`.

Contributions from multiple patterns are added. A molecule matching both
patterns can be counted twice, and a complex matching several `Species`
patterns can contribute once for each pattern. In the example,
`Roverlap =` `{python} f'{initial.observables["Roverlap"][0]:g}'`, since a
ligand-bound phosphorylated receptor contributes to both patterns.
Use disjoint patterns or an expression with an overlap correction when
the desired measurement is a union of sets.

## Reaction rules and graph changes {#sec-bngl-rules}

A reaction rule gives reactant patterns, an arrow, product patterns, and a
rate law. An optional label precedes the reactants.

| Rule form | Rate-law entries |
|---|---|
| `label: reactants -> products k` | One forward rate law |
| `label: reactants <-> products kf,kr` | Forward and reverse rate laws |
| `0 -> A() ks` | Source with no molecular reactant |
| `A() -> 0 kd` | Deletion |
| `A() -> A() + B() ks` | Template-dependent production of `B` |
| `A(x) + B(y) <-> A(x!1).B(y!1) kon,koff` | Intermolecular association and dissociation |
| `A(Y~u) -> A(Y~p) kp` | Internal-state change |

The plus sign separates reactant or product species patterns. Each
occurrence represents a species instance. Thus `A() + A()` requests two
reactant instances, while a dotted pattern can select molecules within
one complex. Intracomplex bond formation can be represented with a dotted
reactant pattern selecting components already in the same complex.

On the product side, BioNetGen changes the molecular properties named by
the rule and retains the surrounding molecular context. When a new molecule is created,
the product must specify the components and internal states needed to
identify it. With repeated molecule types or an ambiguous transformation,
use consistent molecule tags on both sides and inspect the generated
reactions to check the correspondence.

Rules that overlap contribute additional reaction channels. A more
specific rule does not automatically replace a general rule matching the
same molecules. Partition contexts if different rates are intended for
mutually exclusive cases.

### Deletion and rule modifiers {#sec-bngl-modifiers}

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "deletion", "begin reaction rules", "end reaction rules")
```

For a bound `R`–`L` seed complex, `LoseComplex` removes the entire complex.
`LoseReceptor` removes the matched receptor and its incident bond, leaving
the ligand as a free molecule. `DeleteMolecules` is therefore needed when
unmentioned partners should survive deletion. A rule that explicitly
retains a partner on the product side can also specify that survival.

| Modifier | Meaning and scope |
|---|---|
| `DeleteMolecules` | Delete specified molecules while retaining unmentioned partners, which can become separate product species |
| `MoveConnected` | A transported molecule carries connected, unmentioned molecules in its original compartment |
| `TotalRate` | NFsim interprets a global functional rate as a total rule rate; see @sec-bngl-functional for the tested network behavior |
| `include_reactants(i,pattern)` | Require a matching pattern in the whole species selected by reactant position `i` |
| `exclude_reactants(i,pattern)` | Reject a matching pattern in that reactant species |
| `include_products(i,pattern)` | Apply an inclusion filter to the generated product species at position `i` |
| `exclude_products(i,pattern)` | Apply an exclusion filter to that product species |

Modifiers follow the rate law. Positions in the filter arguments begin at
one and refer to the plus-separated patterns. Keep filter argument lists
free of spaces, as in `exclude_reactants(1,R(l!+))`. A filter examines the
whole selected species, so in a multireceptor complex it may find a
different receptor from the one transformed by the rule. Explicit local
context is preferable when the requirement concerns the reacting receptor.

The parser also accepts `priority=value`. Rule priority is used in
specialized workflows and should not be interpreted as a general override
of overlapping kinetic rules across simulators.

## Functions and rate-law conventions {#sec-bngl-functional}

A global function has the form `name() = expression`. It can use
parameters, observables, other functions, and simulation time. Calling
that function as a rule's rate law ordinarily supplies a rate coefficient:
the generated reaction still multiplies the function by its reactant
amounts and statistical factors.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "functional_rates", "begin functions", "end reaction rules")
```

For `Coefficient`, the reaction flux is `rate()*Atotal`. Since the seed
amount of `A` is fixed, the example has a constant coefficient and a
constant source of `B`. `SourceFlux` has no reactant multiplier, so its
flux is `rate()`.

::: {.callout-note}
## `TotalRate` depends on the simulation backend

In NFsim, `TotalFlux` uses `rate()` as a total rule rate. In the tested
network export, `TotalFlux` and `Coefficient` receive the same functional
coefficient in the `.net` file, and the ODE simulation multiplies both
by `Atotal`. The native ODE run therefore gives
`Btotal =` `{python} f'{fd["Btotal"][-1]:g}'`,
`Ctotal =` `{python} f'{fd["Ctotal"][-1]:g}'`, and
`Dtotal =` `{python} f'{fd["Dtotal"][-1]:g}'` at its final time.

For a network-based source whose flux is a function of an observable,
use `0 -> product function()`, as in `SourceFlux`. When a rule also
consumes reactants, derive a rate coefficient that gives the intended
flux and remains defined over the reachable states. The parser rejects
`TotalRate` combined with a local function or `Arrhenius` law.
:::

### Local functions and tags

A local function takes a reference to a matched complex or molecule.
Within that function, `Observable(x)` evaluates the observable with the
scope or root specified by `x`.

| Tag | Reference |
|---|---|
| `%x:R()` | The whole complex matched by this species pattern |
| `%x@membrane:R()` | The whole complex, with a species-level compartment constraint |
| `R%x()` | The particular matched receptor molecule |

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "local_complex", "begin functions", "end reaction rules")
show_lines("appendix_b", "local_molecule", "Phos:", comments=False)
```

In both files, `Bound` is the motif `R(l!1).L(r!1)` and the seed complex
contains a dimer with ligand on one receptor. The species-level tag lets
each reacting receptor see the bound motif anywhere in that complex.
The molecule-level tag roots the observable match at the tagged receptor,
so the unbound receptor receives the base rate and the bound receptor
receives the enhanced rate. A molecule reference therefore imposes more
than a restriction to the containing complex; the observable's root must
match that molecule.

`FunctionProduct("f(x)","g(y)")` provides a specialized product of local
functions on separate reactants for network-free models. Keep each factor
dependent on its own reactant reference and check support in the selected
simulator. For ordinary network generation, many local expressions expand
to reaction-specific coefficients once each reactant species is known.

### Specialized network rate laws

The parser retains built-in rate forms used by older models:

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "specialized_rates", "begin reaction rules", "end reaction rules")
```

| Form | Convention for the illustrated unit-stoichiometry reaction |
|---|---|
| `Sat(v,K)` | $v[A]/(K+[A])$ for the first reactant; additional reactants multiply the rate |
| `Hill(v,K,n)` | $v[B]^n/(K^n+[B]^n)$ for the first reactant; additional reactants multiply the rate |
| `MM(kcat,K)` | Substrate first, enzyme second; uses a free-substrate estimate from total substrate and enzyme |

`MM` has a specific total-substrate convention, so substituting a familiar
Michaelis–Menten formula without checking the represented pools can change
the kinetics. A `Sat` law can have further saturation constants associated
with subsequent reactants. These forms refer to explicit generated
reactant species, which can differ from a saturation function of a pooled
observable. They are also less portable across simulators and exporters
than explicit functions. State the intended flux mathematically before
translating a specialized form to a functional coefficient.

## Compartments and transport {#sec-bngl-compartments}

Each compartment line has the form `name dimension size [outside]`.
The dimension is `3` for a volume or `2` for a surface compartment;
`outside` names its enclosing compartment. BioNetGen uses the containment
tree to check bonds and transport between neighboring locations.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "compartments", "begin compartments", "end compartments")
show_bngl("appendix_b", "compartments", "begin seed species", "end reaction rules")
```

`@inside:A()` sets a species-level compartment, while `A()@inside`
specifies the molecule's compartment. A pattern can also specify molecule
locations within a complex that spans adjacent compartments. The
containment tree restricts which cross-compartment bonds are allowed.

Compartmental rates can acquire volume conversion factors, and a surface
compartment's size is used with BioNetGen's compartment convention.
Record whether a membrane size represents an effective volume, for example
surface area times an assigned width, and keep its units consistent with
the amount convention. Dimension `2` alone does not supply that width.

For transport, a species-level location change can move a matched complex
according to the compartment rules. A molecule-level location change
selects the named molecule; `MoveConnected` specifies how unmentioned
connected molecules in its original compartment accompany it. Check
the generated products for complexes spanning several compartments,
since movement can change the allowed topology.

## Energy patterns {#sec-bngl-energy}

An energy-pattern line has the form `pattern energy_expression`. Its
contribution is multiplied by the number of occurrences of the pattern,
with pattern symmetry accounted for, and added to the species energy.
The energies used by `Arrhenius` are dimensionless free energies.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "energy_binding", "begin energy patterns", "end reaction rules")
```

`Arrhenius(phi,Ea)` supplies both directions of a reversible rule, so it
has no second comma-separated reverse rate law. For an energy difference
$\Delta g$, the numerical coefficients are

$$
k_+=e^{-E_a-\phi\Delta g},\qquad
k_-=e^{-E_a+(1-\phi)\Delta g}.
$$

The energy difference fixes their ratio, while `Ea` sets the kinetic scale
and `phi` allocates the energy change between the directions. Association
energies require a concentration reference, and the rates require a time
reference. In this example `gbind = ln(KD/Cref)` uses the micromolar
reference recorded in the file. The parameter `Cref` is part of that
expression; it does not independently request a unit conversion from
BioNetGen. The older `setOption("energyBNG",1)` command is deprecated
because energy-pattern syntax is enabled by default in the tested release.

## Network generation {#sec-bngl-network}

`generate_network({options})` iteratively applies the rules to the seed
species and newly generated species. It writes an enumerated `.net`
file when network generation succeeds.

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `overwrite=>1` | Allow an existing output network to be replaced |
| `max_iter=>value` | Limit successive rounds of rule application |
| `max_agg=>value` | Limit the total number of molecules in a generated species |
| `max_stoich=>{R=>value,L=>value}` | Limit the number of each named molecule type in a generated species |
| `check_iso=>1` | Check molecular graph isomorphism when identifying species |
| `prefix=>"name"`, `suffix=>"name"` | Control output names |

An aggregate or stoichiometry limit changes which species and reactions
are included. It therefore defines a truncated model whose predictions
require a convergence check as the limit is increased. An iteration limit
can also stop enumeration before the network closes. For a model with
unbounded polymerization, network-free simulation avoids enumeration of
the complete species set.

The generated network contains indexed parameters, functions, species,
reactions, and observable groups. A reaction's comment identifies its
originating rule. Its coefficient may contain a statistical factor for
equivalent sites or identical reactants. Compare the generated elementary
rate with the intended event rate before interpreting a rule parameter
as a macroscopic association or dissociation constant.

## Simulation actions {#sec-bngl-simulators}

An action uses the form `simulate({method=>"method",options})`.

| Method | Simulation |
|---|---|
| `"ode"` | Deterministic ODE integration of an enumerated network |
| `"ssa"` | Stochastic simulation of an enumerated network |
| `"pla"` | Partitioned-leaping approximation for a network |
| `"psa"` | Partial-scaling approximate stochastic network simulation |
| `"nf"` | NFsim simulation directly from the rule-based model |

For network methods, generate the network before simulating. NFsim uses
the molecular types, rules, and seeds exported to XML and can run without
`generate_network()`. An NFsim input must satisfy the simulator's feature
requirements; accepting a file in the BNGL parser does not establish
support for every rate law.

| Option | Meaning and applicability |
|---|---|
| `t_start`, `t_end` | Requested time interval; use an explicit start in multistage protocols |
| `n_steps` | Number of output intervals, with the initial point also reported |
| `sample_times=>[times]` | Requested output times; use this instead of `n_steps` |
| `atol`, `rtol` | Absolute and relative tolerances for ODE integration |
| `sparse=>1` | Sparse linear algebra for the ODE solver |
| `seed=>integer` | Random seed for stochastic methods |
| `suffix=>"name"` | Distinguish output files from separate runs |
| `continue=>1` | Append a network-simulation continuation using its current state and time; retain the same output prefix |
| `print_functions=>1` | Request global-function output |
| `steady_state=>1` | Enable the network ODE solver's steady-state stopping criterion |
| `get_final_state=>1` | Request the final NFsim state, including molecular species output |

Output intervals are observation intervals, not the internal integration
steps or stochastic event times. Specifying `n_steps` together with
`sample_times` gives precedence to `n_steps` and produces a warning.
Use distinct suffixes for independent runs and reset the molecular amounts
between them. Set `t_start` explicitly when switching to NFsim after a
previous simulation; NFsim otherwise uses the model's current time.
NFsim reports elapsed time and rejects `continue=>1` in the tested release.

For reproducible stochastic runs, record the simulator version and seed.
The same seed in SSA and NFsim does not imply the same trajectory, since
the algorithms sample different event representations.

## Parameter changes, protocols, and scans {#sec-bngl-protocols}

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| `setParameter("name","expression")` | Change a defined parameter |
| `setConcentration("complete_species","expression")` | Set the amount of an existing species |
| `addConcentration("complete_species","expression")` | Add to its current amount |
| `saveParameters("label")` | Save current parameter definitions under a label |
| `resetParameters("label")` | Restore those saved definitions |
| `saveConcentrations("label")` | Save the current species amounts |
| `resetConcentrations("label")` | Restore the saved amounts |
| `resetConcentrations()` | Restore default seed amounts |
| `setVolume("compartment","expression")` | Change a declared compartment size |

Species addressed by concentration actions must already exist in the
species list; an action does not create a missing species definition.
Changing a seed parameter after simulation and restoring seed amounts
is distinct from directly setting the current amount. Parameter and
concentration saves are separate, so restore both when an experiment
changes both. A concentration reset also leaves time management to the
simulation action; specify the intended start explicitly.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "actions", 'saveConcentrations("start")',
          'resetParameters("rates")')
```

`parameter_scan` runs a sequence of parameter values and records the
final observables for each value:

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_lines("appendix_b", "actions", "parameter_scan(", comments=False)
```

| Scan option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `parameter=>"name"` | Defined parameter to vary |
| `par_min`, `par_max`, `n_scan_pts` | Endpoints and number of scan values |
| `log_scale=>1` | Logarithmic spacing; endpoints must be positive |
| `par_scan_vals=>[values]` | Explicit values instead of a regularly spaced range |
| `reset_conc=>1` | Start scan points from the saved starting amounts |
| `reset_conc=>0` | Carry final amounts into the next point |
| `method`, `t_end`, `n_steps` | Simulation options used at each scan point |

Independent dose-response scans and scans that carry state between points
answer different questions, particularly in models with multiple stable
states. Restore parameters after a scan if subsequent actions require the
original values. `bifurcate` automates increasing and decreasing scans
with carried state; its result still depends on sufficient relaxation at
each point.

`readFile({file=>"model.bngl"})` reads another BNGL file;
`readFile({file=>"network.net"})` reads a generated network. Relative
paths are interpreted within the execution environment, so keep supporting
files with a documented run directory. SBML import is a separate translation
workflow and can require additional Atomizer dependencies.

## Exports, visualization, and output files {#sec-bngl-output}

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
show_bngl("appendix_b", "actions", "writeModel(")
```

| Action | Representation written |
|---|---|
| `writeModel()` | BNGL model definition |
| `writeNetwork()` | Enumerated `.net` reaction network |
| `writeXML()` | BioNetGen's rule-based XML, including NFsim input |
| `writeSBML()` | SBML representation of the reaction network |
| `writeSBMLMulti()` | Structured SBML Multi export, with feature-dependent support |
| `writeMfile()` | MATLAB simulation code |
| `writeMexfile()` | MATLAB interface and C source for a compiled solver |
| `writeMDL()` | MCell-oriented export for supported models |
| `visualize({type=>"contactmap"})` | Molecule types, components, and possible bonds |
| `visualize({type=>"ruleviz_pattern"})` | Reactant and product patterns of rules |
| `visualize({type=>"ruleviz_operation"})` | Graph operations performed by rules |
| `visualize({type=>"regulatory"})` | Relationships between rules and their structural requirements |

Most writers accept output-name options such as `suffix`. Visualization
writes graph files for a separate layout program. Regulatory graphs can
use options including `groups`, `collapse`, and an `opts` file defining
user groupings. An exporter may require network generation or reject
constructs it cannot represent. `writeXML` and `writeSBML` both write XML
files but encode different model representations; use distinct suffixes
when requesting both.

| Extension | Contents |
|---|---|
| `.bngl` | Rule-based model and requested actions |
| `.net` | Enumerated species, reactions, functions, and observable weights |
| `.gdat` | Time and observable values, usually with a `#` header |
| `.cdat` | Time and individual network-species amounts |
| `.fdat` | Global function values when written separately by a network backend; some backends append them to `.gdat` |
| `.species` | Final molecular species and counts from NFsim |
| `.scan` | Parameter values and final observables from a scan |
| `.graphml`, `.gml` | Graph representations produced by visualization; the tested contact-map export uses GraphML |

Read the header to identify output columns; species indices can change
when a model is edited or its network is regenerated. Use observables
with stable names for analyses that compare model versions.

## Diagnosing syntax and execution errors

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| Undefined parameter or function | Spelling, case, definition order, and parentheses on function calls |
| Missing component or internal state in a seed | Write a complete species consistent with its molecule type |
| Illegal bond wildcard in a seed | Replace pattern wildcards with a specified bond or an unbound component |
| Unmatched bond endpoint | Each explicit bond label must identify both endpoints within the expression |
| Missing reverse rate law | Supply both coefficients for `<->`, except when using `Arrhenius` |
| Species not found in a concentration action | Generate the species or include it as a seed before addressing it |
| Unexpected receptor or complex count | Compare `Molecules` with `Species` and check overlapping patterns |
| Unexpected rate multiplicity | Inspect equivalent sites, repeated reactants, local-function scope, and generated statistical factors |
| No network closure | Check for unbounded aggregation or an iteration limit |
| Simulation interval error | Check the current time and supply explicit `t_start` and `t_end` |
| Unrecognized action option | Check the spelling and the options accepted by the selected method |

Parser errors identify the file and line being read. Reduce the failing
rule or pattern to a small executable model before changing the full
model; the examples in this appendix provide starting points for checking
matching, counting, and rate semantics.

## Additional language constructs and source locations

Population molecule types, `population maps`, and
`generate_hybrid_model` support hybrid particle/population workflows.
They require a deliberate mapping between particle structures and
population variables. Time-indexed tabular functions, including `tfun`
in newer source snapshots, also have version-dependent syntax and
backend support. Those specialized workflows should be checked against
the distribution being used rather than inferred from a parser keyword.

The implementation files provide the detailed reference for less common
constructs. All links below point to the source snapshot used for this
draft.

- [Model blocks and core actions](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/BNGModel.pm)
  define file processing, network generation, and parameter changes.
- [Molecular graphs](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/SpeciesGraph.pm)
  and [components](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/Component.pm)
  define pattern syntax and graph attributes.
- [Observables](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/Observable.pm)
  define counting and quantifiers.
- [Reaction rules](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/RxnRule.pm)
  and [rate laws](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/RateLaw.pm)
  define transformations and rate modifiers.
- [Expressions](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/Expression.pm)
  define mathematical operators and built-in functions.
- [Simulation actions](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/bng2/Perl2/BNGAction.pm)
  define method options, protocols, and scans.

The [upstream quick-reference guide](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen/blob/9601746f8884ed19ab2acea49fe87fc4660ace46/docs/assets/QRG-30Mar2016.pdf)
provides earlier examples of the language. Its installation instructions
and some simulator details reflect the release available when it was
written.
